questions.text: No single crop or product gave more than 70 percent of our sales income last year.
We have a written business plan with targets and a budget for the next 1 to 3 years, and we reviewed it in the last 12 months.
Before each season we check which crop or product has a ready buyer and a positive margin, and we choose what to plant, process or stock on that basis.
We have a written agreement (offtake, supply or purchase) with at least one buyer, covering volume, price basis and quality.
In the last 12 months we delivered at least 95 percent of the volume our buyers ordered, on the agreed dates.
No single buyer took more than half of our sales last year.
Our buyers paid us on the agreed date for most deliveries in the last season.
Before agreeing a selling price, we check current prices from at least two sources, such as markets, buyers, aggregators or a price information service.
We have a plan for when to sell, such as selling in stages or storing for a better price, and we did not sell all our produce at the harvest glut last season.
We sell part of our produce after cleaning, grading, shelling, drying or processing, so that we earn more than the raw farm-gate price.
We check every lot we buy or collect for moisture and for foreign or damaged material before we accept it.
We can show a buyer where each lot came from (member or farm, village and date of purchase).
Our last delivery to our main buyer passed the buyer's quality check without rejection or price cut.
We write a plan before each season showing area per crop, expected yield, and the inputs, labour and money we will need.
We know our own average yield per acre for our main crop over the last 3 seasons, from records and not from guesswork.
Most of the area we plant each season uses certified or improved seed of varieties suited to our rainfall, bought from a registered seller.
For our main crop we follow the planting time, spacing and fertiliser rate advised by extension or the seed or fertiliser supplier, and we can show what we did.
We receive the seed, fertiliser and chemicals we need before planting time in most seasons, without delays that cost us yield.
We buy inputs from known registered suppliers and compare prices or terms from at least two before we buy.
We record who received which inputs from us, how much, and what each person still owes.
We buy sealed, labelled seed, fertiliser and chemicals from licensed sellers, and we check the label and expiry date before use or resale.
We dry and clean produce to the buyer's or national moisture standard before storing or selling, and we measure moisture to confirm.
Our store is clean, dry and off the ground with a written pest control routine that we follow.
We have measured how much produce we lost after harvest in the last season and can name the main causes.
We rotate stock first in, first out, and the oldest lots are sold or processed before newer ones.
We keep a business bank account or business mobile money wallet separate from personal or household money, and business money passes through it.
We write every sale and every expense in a cash book, notebook or app within one week of it happening.
We can show written records of sales, costs and loan repayments for the last 2 to 3 seasons.
At any time we can say how much buyers or members owe us, and how much we owe suppliers and lenders, from written lists.
We prepare a month-by-month cash plan across the season showing when money will come in and go out.
We know how much money we need before harvest (for weeding, labour, hired services and household needs) and where it will come from.
We keep a cash or savings reserve that could cover at least one month of running costs in the lean season.
At least once each season we compare our cash plan with actual cash in and out, and change our plan when the two differ.
We have recorded the full cost of production per acre for our main crop in the last season, including labour, inputs and hired services.
We know the profit per acre, or per bag, kg or litre, for each of our main crops or products from last season.
We know our break-even price per bag or kg, and we do not sell below it unless the leaders or owner decide so.
An independent person (an auditor, accountant or trained reviewer who is not the book-keeper) checks our accounts at least once a year.
The person who receives cash is not the same person who records it or who approves large payments.
In the last 3 years we repaid every loan (bank, microfinance, input credit or group loan) in full and by the due date, shown by lender records.
Repayment dates on any loan match when we get paid, such as after harvest sales, and not before.
Money we borrow is used for what we said it was for, and we keep receipts showing how loan money was spent.
Our yearly loan repayments take less than a third of our yearly net income in a normal season.
Our savings group or cooperative savings follow written rules on shares, loans, interest and fines, and the rules are linked to the group's farming or business activity.
We have used at least two different sources of finance in the last 2 years, such as a bank, microfinance, VSLA, supplier credit, buyer advance or asset finance.
We know the terms of any input credit, buyer advance or outgrower deal we take, including interest or price deduction, and these are written down.
We have used or checked a warehouse receipt, asset finance or lease option for equipment or storage, and we know the requirements to qualify.
We prepare yearly financial statements (income statement, balance sheet and cash flow) that a lender or investor could read.
We hold a written list of our assets (land, equipment, buildings, stock) with their approximate value and who owns each.
We hold documents that a lender would accept as security, such as land documents, warehouse receipts, stock records or a buyer contract assignment.
We have a written funding request showing how much we need, what it will buy, how it will earn money, and when it will be repaid.
If the owner, manager or chairperson is away for two weeks, another named person can run buying, selling and payments using written instructions.
Our owner, manager or leaders completed training in business, farm or group management in the last 2 years, and we can show it.
We have a written plan for who leads or owns the enterprise or group if the current leader leaves, falls ill or dies.
Our members elect leaders at a general meeting, and each member has one vote.
Most members attend our general meetings, and each year they receive a report on money, sales and decisions.
Most members sell most of their crop through the group, and we know how much they sold elsewhere.
The roles of owner or board, managers and staff or members, and who can approve spending and sign contracts, are written down and followed.
No child below 15 works in our enterprise or on our farm, and no one under 18 does hazardous work such as spraying chemicals or carrying heavy loads.
In the last 12 months our staff, members or workers received training in a skill we need, such as good farming practice, storage or record keeping, with an attendance list.
An extension officer, agronomist or technical adviser visited our farms or members at least once in the last season, and we recorded the advice.
Members or outgrowers who take group inputs or credit repay on time, and we keep a record of who owes what.
We pay the farmers, members or suppliers who sell to us on the date we promised, and they receive a payment slip or message.
Members, outgrowers, workers and suppliers have a known way to raise a complaint, and we record and answer complaints.
We keep a register of the farms or plots we farm or buy from, showing the owner, crop, area in acres and where the plot is.
We keep batch and stock records that show what came in, what went out and what is in the store, updated each time stock moves.
We give a receipt or delivery note for every sale or purchase, and keep a copy.
We keep important records (contracts, receipts, member lists, accounts) for at least 2 years in a safe place, with a copy kept elsewhere.
We use mobile money or bank transfers to pay farmers and workers, and to receive payment from buyers, for most of our transactions.
We keep our records on a phone app, spreadsheet or computer system, with backups, and not only on paper.
Each month we compare our mobile money or bank statement with our own records and explain any difference.
Passwords, PINs and signing rights for our accounts and wallets are held only by authorised people and are not shared informally.
Leaders or owners review sales, costs, stock and loan balances at least monthly in a meeting or written note.
We track at least five measures with targets, such as yield per acre, cost per bag, deliveries on time, repayment rate and post-harvest loss.
We collect data from our members, outgrowers or suppliers each season (area, expected and actual output, inputs received) and use it to plan.
Last season's results changed something we did this season, and we can name the change and the result that led to it.
Our business, farm group or cooperative is legally registered with the right body (Registrar General or Department of Cooperatives) and the registration is current.
We have a Tax Identification Number and we filed the tax returns that apply to us on time in the last year.
We hold written proof of our right to use the land we farm or store on (lease, allocation letter, customary grant record or title), covering at least the next 3 years.
We know whether our farming or processing activity qualifies for a tax incentive, and we have claimed what applies to us.
We hold the current registrations, licences and permits that our activity needs from the agencies that regulate us (for example FDA, EPA, PPRSD, TCDA or Department of Cooperatives).
We hold a TCDA export permit and proof of payment of the development levy before each export shipment of raw shea or cashew.
Our store or processing site and the food products we sell meet FDA requirements for what we do (licence, premises, labelling and records).

We are certified, or following a written plan with dates to be certified, for the standard our target markets require (for example organic, Fairtrade, GlobalG.A.P. or the Global Shea Alliance programme).
At least once a year we check our own practices against the standard or buyer rules we follow, and fix what we find.
We use only registered pesticides, applied by trained people wearing protective gear, and we record what was applied, where and when.
We have a written list of the main risks to our enterprise (weather, price, theft, buyer default, illness) with at least one action for each.
We have insurance on at least one major risk to our crop, livestock, stock or equipment, and we know what the policy covers.
Before we sell on credit or give inputs on credit to a new customer or member, we check their record and set a credit limit in writing.
We have a written plan with at least two actions for a dry spell, flood or pest outbreak, such as early maturing seed, staggered planting or a second income.
Each season we obtain the seasonal rainfall forecast or weather advisory (for example from the Ghana Meteorological Agency or a radio or phone service) and use it to time planting and other work.
Last season we spread risk by planting on staggered dates, or by planting drought or heat tolerant varieties on part of our area.
We keep a record of weather and pest shocks (dry spells, floods, outbreaks) and their cost to us in each of the last 3 seasons.
We have a plan to look after our land, trees and water, for example tree planting, soil care and no bush burning, and we followed it last season.
On most of our area we use practices that keep soil fertile, such as legume rotation, manure or compost, crop residue cover or contour ridges.
Our farm, processing site or store holds the EPA registration or permit that its size and activity require, or EPA has confirmed in writing that none is needed.
We dispose of waste from our farm or site (empty chemical containers, processing waste, plastic) safely, away from water sources and food.
Women who farm with us, supply us or work for us take part in decisions and have a say in how money from sales is used.
Women who farm with us can own or use the land, trees, tools and equipment they need through our group or enterprise, in their own name or jointly.
Women hold leadership roles or sit on committees, and at least one third of leaders or managers are women.
Young people (aged 18 to 35) have defined roles or paid work with us, such as in production, aggregation, processing or records, and we know how many.
